article_title: Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011-2014
citation: Reedy, K., & Lacireno-Paquet, N. (2015). Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011–2014. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.kansasmtss.org/pdf/ex_eval/2015_KS_MTSS_Eval_Report.pdf
title: Kansas MTSS framework: a system-level change framework integrating core components for academic and behavioral outcomes
description: The Kansas MTSS is a statewide framework aiming to improve outcomes for all students through system-level change across classroom, school, district, and state. It integrates effective-schools components into "a single framework for improved social and academic outcomes for all students." Core components include evidence-based curriculum, high-quality instruction, a comprehensive assessment system, data-based decision making, effective intervention, fidelity of implementation, ongoing professional development, and empowering leadership culture. Implementation features "frequent data-based monitoring for instructional decision making" and a continuum of evidence-based systemwide practices enabling rapid response to each student's needs.
requirements: Evidence-based curriculum and high-quality core instruction and assessment
Data-based decision making supported by a comprehensive assessment system
Ongoing professional development and leadership within an empowering school and district culture
Fidelity of implementation
constraints: Sustaining implementation requires staff buy-in, institutionalization of MTSS practices, and sustained district and school leadership support; training, flexible scheduling, and resource purchases are necessary but not sufficient
target_learners: All K-12 students in participating Kansas public schools
target_learning_goals: Improved academic outcomes in reading and math
Improved behavioral outcomes and reduced special education referrals
examples: More than a third of all Kansas public schools were implementing MTSS, used as a key approach for turning around low-performing schools in the state
key_sources: Reedy, K., & Lacireno-Paquet, N. (2015). Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011–2014. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.kansasmtss.org/pdf/ex_eval/2015_KS_MTSS_Eval_Report.pdf

article_title: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report-2014
citation: Kristin Reedy, Ed.D., and Natalie Lacireno-Paquet, Ph.D. (2015). Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report—2014. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Kansas MTSS framework: a system-level change framework integrating core components for academic and behavioral outcomes
description: The Kansas MTSS framework aims to improve outcomes for all students through system-level change across classroom, school, district, and state, using "a coherent continuum of evidence based, system-wide practices to support a rapid response to each student's academic and behavioral needs" with frequent data-based monitoring. Its core components are evidence-based curriculum, high-quality instruction, a comprehensive assessment system, data-based decision making, effective intervention, fidelity of implementation, ongoing professional development, and leadership within an empowering culture. Curriculum, instruction, and assessment form the core supporting all students, supported in turn by leadership, professional development, and an empowering culture.
requirements: Implementation with fidelity requires systems change, including school- and district-level leadership, ongoing professional development, and alignment of school improvement initiatives under the MTSS framework
constraints: The report notes implementing MTSS with fidelity is challenged by staff and leadership turnover, secondary-level course and credit constraints, scheduling time, integrating multiple content areas, and staff skill in designing intensive interventions
target_learners: all K-12 students in participating Kansas public schools
target_learning_goals: improved academic outcomes in reading and math
improved student behavior
examples: Case study schools operated building leadership teams, three-times-per-year universal screening, weekly grade-level data review, and daily intervention blocks with groups regrouped based on screening and progress-monitoring data
key_sources: Kristin Reedy, Ed.D., and Natalie Lacireno-Paquet, Ph.D. (2015). Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report—2014. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559729

article_title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: kar2ouche storyboarding tool for visualizing Macbeth
description: kar2ouche is "an electronic storyboarding tool, which allows pupils to construct their own visual representations of Macbeth in a series of frames". Pupils insert characters, pictures and backgrounds, adjust size, position and pose, and add speech bubbles (for Shakespeare's dialogue), thought bubbles (for their interpretation), and a caption box (for their reasons). It computerises traditional storyboarding to simplify frame construction and make Shakespeare more enjoyable, while supporting exam preparation.
requirements: Teacher introduction covering frame construction, bubble conventions, and caption-box use
Pair arrangement at the computer, the arrangement both study teachers chose
constraints: Used here as one activity within English lessons preparing for Key Stage 3 SATs on Macbeth
target_learning_goals: Close engagement with Shakespeare's text
Creative visual interpretation of scenes
examples: Pupils produced storyboards across lessons; all storyboards were saved and collected after each computer-suite lesson
key_sources: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9134-8

article_title: Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Navarro-Ibáñez, M., Balladares, J., Sprovera, I., Manaut, C., & Infante, M. (2026). Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10208-6
title: Karabenick and Dembo's eight-stage help-seeking model with instrumental versus executive help-seeking
description: The review describes the eight-stage model as "a widely recognized help-seeking model in the literature", which "highlights various cognitive, social, affective-emotional, and contextual competencies required at each stage", from identifying a problem through processing received help. It also presents Nelson-Le Gall's distinction "identifying two types: instrumental (or adaptive) help-seeking and executive (or non-adaptive) help-seeking", where instrumental help-seeking promotes learning and independence while executive help-seeking obtains immediate answers without deepening understanding.
requirements: Learners must deploy cognitive, social, affective-emotional, and contextual competencies across the eight stages, from problem identification to processing received help
constraints: The review notes there is no consensus on the exact structure of help-seeking
target_learning_goals: adaptive (instrumental) help-seeking
metacognitive monitoring of learning needs
examples: The review uses the model to frame how preservice teachers decide whether, whom, and how to ask for help during coursework and practicum
key_sources: Navarro-Ibáñez, M., Balladares, J., Sprovera, I., Manaut, C., & Infante, M. (2026). Help! I Need Somebody: A Systematic Review of Academic Help-Seeking Among Pre-Service Teachers. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10208-6

article_title: A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading tests with over one hundred thousand children.
citation: Monroe, W. S. (1917). A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading Tests with over one hundred thousand children. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Kansas+Silent+Reading+Tests
title: Kansas Silent Reading Tests (Kelly), a three-test objective silent reading series with weighted exercises
description: A silent reading test series devised by F. J. Kelly and distributed by the Bureau of Educational Measurements and Standards. It comprises "Three tests" for grade spans 3-5, 6-8 and 9-12, each consisting of sixteen exercises scored in five minutes. Each exercise has a value proportional to the average time required to do it correctly, and the tests are objective in that "there is little opportunity for differences of opinion in marking the test papers". Rate and comprehension are combined in a single score.
requirements: An examiner able to give directions and maintain standard conditions such as time allowance and physical conditions
constraints: Many exercises are arithmetical puzzle-like items rather than typical reading material, a defect the author could not eliminate
Only one form of the test was available
target_learning_goals: silent reading rate and comprehension
examples: More than 100,000 pupils in 160 cities were tested in 1915-'16 and 1916-'17; adult groups such as teachers at institutes scored medians of roughly 18.5 to 40.4 in Table III
key_sources: Monroe, W. S. (1917). A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading Tests with over one hundred thousand children. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Kansas+Silent+Reading+Tests

article_title: Can tablet apps support the learning of handwriting? An investigation of learning outcomes in kindergarten classroom
citation: Nathalie Bonneton-Botté, Sylvain Fleury, Nathalie Girard, Maëlys Le Magadou, Anthony Cherbonnier, Mickaël Renault, Eric Anquetil, Eric Jamet. (2020). Can Tablet Apps Support the Learning of Handwriting? An Investigation of Learning Outcomes in Kindergarten Classroom. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103831
title: Kaligo digital notebook app for stylus-oriented tablets
description: Kaligo is a digital workbook developed in the IntuiScript project that gives children realtime extrinsic feedback (knowledge of results) each time they write a letter, digit or word. Basic feedback covers "shape, direction, order of the strokes and continuity", shown as a colored horseshoe gauge with a star when production is sufficiently like the model. Its AI analyzes spatiotemporal handwriting features, adapts pedagogical scenarios automatically, and stores productions in a dashboard teachers use to program personalized exercises.
requirements: Stylus-oriented tablet hardware (Galaxy Tab A with S Pen was used)
Automatic handwriting analysis tuned to pedagogical recommendations; the article states it was demonstrated equivalent to teacher assessment
constraints: Feedback is delivered only on completion of each trial, not during the writing movement
Connection times were not reliable enough in the trial to infer actual durations of use
target_learners: kindergarten beginning writers (5–6 year olds) learning cursive writing
target_learning_goals: acquisition of legible, fluent cursive handwriting (letter shape, stroke order, direction, size)
examples: Nine kindergarten teachers used Kaligo's "I write in capitals" and "I write in cursive" modules for about 20 minutes per child per week over 12 weeks, supplementing with paper or whiteboard writing activities
key_sources: Nathalie Bonneton-Botté, Sylvain Fleury, Nathalie Girard, Maëlys Le Magadou, Anthony Cherbonnier, Mickaël Renault, Eric Anquetil, Eric Jamet. (2020). Can Tablet Apps Support the Learning of Handwriting? An Investigation of Learning Outcomes in Kindergarten Classroom. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103831

article_title: An artificial intelligence application framework for nursing education: a scoping review based on the KAS model.
citation: Xiang Yue, Shi Haoning, Ren Keke, Yang Xilin, Li Lin, Zhao Qinghua, Huang Huanhuan. (2026). An artificial intelligence application framework for nursing education: a scoping review based on the KAS model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09209-4
title: KAS-based AI application framework for nursing education with three primary dimensions and twelve sub-dimensions
description: The review proposes an AI application framework for nursing education grounded in the Knowledge-Attitude-Skill model, refining three primary dimensions into twelve secondary sub-dimensions (K1–K4, A1–A4, S1–S4). The article states that "By refining the three dimensions of knowledge, attitudes, and skills into 12 specific sub-dimensions, it offers educators clear guidance for systematically designing teaching objectives, organizing instructional content, and conducting teaching evaluations." It was built through a deductive-inductive hybrid coding of 23 included studies.
requirements: Existing frameworks must be synthesized across general, medical, and other professional education contexts to provide theoretical scaffolding
constraints: The framework requires ongoing updates because rapid AI advancement necessitates maintaining timeliness; it has not yet been empirically validated
target_learning_goals: AI competency across knowledge, attitude, and skill dimensions
examples: The review mapped 23 included studies onto the twelve sub-dimensions in Table 3 and Fig. 2 to show distribution and emphasis across KAS dimensions
key_sources: Xiang Yue, Shi Haoning, Ren Keke, Yang Xilin, Li Lin, Zhao Qinghua, Huang Huanhuan. (2026). An artificial intelligence application framework for nursing education: a scoping review based on the KAS model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09209-4

article_title: Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class
citation: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Kahoot game-based Classroom Response System with timed point scoring and a leaderboard
description: Kahoot is a popular game-based Classroom Response System, introduced in 2013, accessible via smartphones or PCs, that instructors use to check learners' knowledge and increase involvement. Students register at https://kahoot.it with a game pin and a chosen username, questions are shown on screen via an overhead projector in real time, and "The total scores for each question are 1,000 points", awarded by time usage and correctness, with total scores displayed from most to least at the quiz's end. In this study it delivered ten vocabulary and five grammar revision quizzes to the experimental group.
requirements: Instructors create an account and can formulate questions or quizzes or borrow those already created by others
Students need a device (smartphone or PC) to register and join with a game pin
target_learners: first- and second-year university EFL students
target_learning_goals: grammar and vocabulary revision
engagement and attention
examples: Ten vocabulary quizzes and five grammar quizzes were delivered via Kahoot to the experimental group while the control group did the same quizzes on paper
key_sources: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1170635

article_title: Analyzing the Efficacy of the Testing Effect Using Kahoot™ on Student Performance
citation: Iwamoto, D. H., Hargis, J., Taitano, E. J., & Vuong, K. (2017). Analyzing the efficacy of the testing effect using Kahoot on student performance. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 18(2). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Kahoot game-show-style online quizzing application
description: Kahoot is an Internet-based quizzing application in which quizzes are presented in a "game-show" type format: students join anonymously via any browser on a mobile device, answer multiple-choice questions against a preset time (20 seconds in this study), receive immediate feedback on the correct answer, and a leaderboard shows the top five fastest accurate responders. In this study the researcher wrote seven multiple-choice questions per chapter aligned with, but not identical in wording to, the high-stakes exam's key concepts, and quiz results carried no course-grade impact.
requirements: Students need Internet-connected mobile devices to log in and respond; quizzes must be authored to align with the key concepts of the upcoming exam
constraints: Quiz results had no impact on the course grade (no-stakes); prior familiarity with Kahoot was noted as a possible confounding variable
target_learning_goals: retention of key course concepts for high-stakes multiple-choice examinations
examples: The experimental section played seven-question chapter quizzes during the final 10 minutes of predetermined classes and replayed all quizzes in a 50-minute review class period
key_sources: Iwamoto, D. H., Hargis, J., Taitano, E. J., & Vuong, K. (2017). Analyzing the efficacy of the testing effect using Kahoot on student performance. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 18(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1145220

article_title: Electronic School Atlas as an Innovative Means of Development of Geographic Education in Kazakhstan Schools
citation: Damekova, S. K., Zharkinbekova, T. N., Turtkarayeva, G. B., Han, S. I., & Damekova, O. Z. (2016). Electronic School Atlas as an Innovative Means of Development of Geographic Education in Kazakhstan Schools. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(18), 12668-12679.
title: Electronic school atlas for Kazakhstan geography education
description: The article introduces an electronic school atlas developed for Kazakhstan schools using the MapWinGIS library and C# 5.0 in Visual Studio 2013. It provides digital vector maps of Kazakhstan with layered display, measurement tools, object search, coordinate reading, multilingual interface (Kazakh, Russian, English), and contour-map creation. The atlas includes 80 maps for the 8th-9th grade geography course and was developed under the project 'The geo-info set of educational maps Atlas' (2013-2015).
requirements: A computer environment running the MapWinGIS library and the atlas software
constraints: Developed specifically for the geography curriculum of Kazakhstan schools
target_learners: Secondary school students in Kazakhstan, grades 6-9
target_learning_goals: Map reading and interpretation
GIS competence
Geographic measurement and analysis
examples: Testing and implementation were carried out in schools #1 and #4 Kokshetau and at the Faculty of Natural Sciences of Sh. Ualikhanov Kokshetau State University
key_sources: Damekova, S. K., Zharkinbekova, T. N., Turtkarayeva, G. B., Han, S. I., & Damekova, O. Z. (2016). article_title: Integrating Technology into ESP Classes: Use of Student Response System in English for Specific Purposes Instruction
citation: Mehmet Asmalı. (2018). Integrating Technology into ESP Classes: Use of Student Response System in English for Specific Purposes Instruction. Teaching English with Technology, 18(3), 86-104. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Kahoot! smartphone clicker application used as the student response system in ESP classes
description: Kahoot! is a smartphone clicker application that lets students join a game with a pin number, answer projected multiple-choice questions by tapping colourful figures on their phones, and see immediate right/wrong feedback and score rankings. It provides instructors with "the detailed report of the overall performance of the students for each week and test", including correct/incorrect percentages, Likert-style feedback, and per-student answer times. In this study it replaced dedicated clicker handsets for 10 weeks of ESP instruction.
requirements: Students need smartphones able to run the application; all students in the study had smart phones equipped to work with the program.
A projector is needed because questions did not appear on the students' phones and had to be watched on the projected screen.
constraints: Users normally choose nicknames, but the study required students to log in with their own names to track points and declare a winner of the day.
target_learners: 2-year vocational school students of tourism and hospitality services
target_learning_goals: ESP vocabulary and communicative language for tourism workplaces
examples: Questions were picture-based, video-based (YouTube clips trimmed to chosen start and end seconds), or classic multiple-choice, each with a 20-second answering window.
key_sources: Mehmet Asmalı. (2018). Integrating Technology into ESP Classes: Use of Student Response System in English for Specific Purposes Instruction. Teaching English with Technology, 18(3), 86-104. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1186385

article_title: The Effect of Second Life on Speaking Achievement
citation: Guzel, S. & Aydin, S. (2016). The effect of second life on speaking achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching. 6(4), 236-245. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1100452
title: Kanatlar (2005) Speaking Grading Scale for oral performance assessment
description: The study used the Speaking Grading Scale (SGS) developed by Kanatlar (2005) to score learners' oral interview performance. The scale "included five different sections to score such as grammar, vocabulary, fluency, intelligibility and task achievement," with a 100-point maximum: 30 points each for grammar and vocabulary, 20 for fluency, and 10 each for intelligibility and task achievement. Two trained research assistants scored pre- and post-test interviews, achieving acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha .80–.88).
requirements: Trained scorers and oral interview tasks; here, TOEFL discussion questions drawn randomly by participants.
constraints: Scores reflect a three-to-four-minute interview performance rather than spontaneous unelicited speech.
target_learners: EFL learners assessed on speaking proficiency
target_learning_goals: Objective measurement of speaking achievement across five skill components
examples: Two ELT research assistants scored each learner's three-to-four-minute TOEFL-topic interview using the SGS.
key_sources: Guzel, S. & Aydin, S. (2016). The effect of second life on speaking achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching. 6(4), 236-245. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED573975

article_title: Construct Validity of Frontier Large Language Models on 4 Spanish Health Professions Specialty-Access Examinations (MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR): Cross-Sectional Benchmarking and Psychometric Study.
citation: Clemente García-Hidalgo, Manuel Carpio-Salmerón, Pau Benito, Carlos Carazo-Casas, Beatriz Carratalá, Jaime Campos Pavón. (2026). Construct Validity of Frontier Large Language Models on 4 Spanish Health Professions Specialty-Access Examinations (MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR): Cross-Sectional Benchmarking and Psychometric Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/106199
title: Kane validity framework applied to LLM examination scores: scoring is supported, but extrapolation to clinical competence and decision-making remain untested
description: The article applies Messick construct-validity framework and Kane's argument-based approach to interpret LLM examination scores, examining "evidence concerning scoring, generalization, and extrapolation, together with construct-irrelevant variance and construct underrepresentation". Table 1 maps four Kane inferences to evidence: scoring is supported for recorded answers against the official key; generalization is limited to these items and configurations; extrapolation shows that "Clinical competence and equivalence with human score interpretations are untested"; and the study does not validate clinical decisions or autonomous educational use. This framework structures the article's central caution that high model accuracy does not by itself establish professional competence.
requirements: Application requires distinguishing expert key agreement from candidate facility, which have different denominators
constraints: The framework's judgments describe the scope of current evidence and do not evaluate the examinations' validity for human candidates
No person-level IRT or formal invariance analysis was performed
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of AI benchmark scores as evidence of professional competence
examples: Table 1 maps scoring, generalization, extrapolation, and decision inferences to the study's evidence and its limits
key_sources: Clemente García-Hidalgo, Manuel Carpio-Salmerón, Pau Benito, Carlos Carazo-Casas, Beatriz Carratalá, Jaime Campos Pavón. (2026). article_title: Nurses' knowledge, attitudes, practices, and educational needs regarding frailty: a multicenter cross-sectional survey in southwestern China.
citation: Lyu Jie, Yang Jun, Kong Ling-Na, Xie Fen, Huang Ying, Liao Ping. (2026). Nurses‚Äô knowledge, attitudes, practices, and educational needs regarding frailty: a multicenter cross-sectional survey in southwestern China. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1920309
title: 31-item knowledge, attitude, and practice of frailty management questionnaire
description: A validated 31-item questionnaire assessing nurses' frailty-management competency across three domains: knowledge (14 items, 14‚Äď42 points), attitude (8 items, 8‚Äď40 points), and practice (9 items, 9‚Äď45 points), with a total score range of 31‚Äď127 where higher scores represent superior competency. The original instrument showed "test‚Äďretest reliability (r‚ÄĮ=‚ÄĮ0.990)" and Cronbach's őĪ of 0.909; in this sample internal consistency was good (total őĪ = 0.930). It was developed via literature review, semi-structured interviews, expert validation, pre-testing, and pilot evaluation.
requirements: Respondents need clinical nursing experience exceeding 1 year and a valid registered nurse license, per the study's inclusion criteria
constraints: Domain percentages of maximum have unequal floors and are not directly comparable across domains, per the article
target_learners: clinical nurses in tertiary general hospitals
target_learning_goals: assessing frailty-management knowledge, attitudes, and practices
examples: Administered anonymously online via the Questionnaire Star platform distributed through WeChat, with completions under 3 minutes and straight-line responding excluded

article_title: Preparedness of dental interns to identify oral potentially malignant disorders and oral cancer: a multi‑state cross‑sectional survey in India.
citation: Misra Satya Ranjan, Das Rupsa, Das Subhra Jyoti. (2026). Preparedness of dental interns to identify oral potentially malignant disorders and oral cancer: a multi-state cross-sectional survey in India. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08681-0
title: Validated KAP questionnaire for assessing dental interns' OPMD and oral cancer preparedness
description: A structured online questionnaire comprising 8 knowledge items (multiple-choice/true-false), 4 attitude statements (5-point Likert), and 3 practice items. Content validity was established by five experts with "item-level content validity index [I-CVI] 0.83–1.00", and it was pilot-tested on 20 interns. Reliability was assessed as KR-20 = 0.62 (knowledge) and Cronbach’s α = 0.88 (attitude).
requirements: Expert panel content validation with I-CVI threshold of 0.78
Pilot testing for clarity and completion time
constraints: Knowledge scale showed modest reliability (KR-20 = 0.62) attributed to few items, heterogeneous content, and easy items producing a ceiling effect
target_learning_goals: Assessing knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding OPMDs and oral cancer early detection
examples: Administered via Google Forms to 1220 interns
key_sources: Misra Satya Ranjan, Das Rupsa, Das Subhra Jyoti. (2026). Preparedness of dental interns to identify oral potentially malignant disorders and oral cancer: a multi-state cross-sectional survey in India. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08681-0

article_title: The effect of web-based learning with peer-facilitated discussion on nursing students' knowledge and practices in work-related biological exposure: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Chen Lulin, Liang Danyan, Zhu Yuhuan, Huang Weihong, Li Chenglin, Liang Xiong, Liang Yutao, Lu Yunyun, Gan Yongjiang, Zhong Yao. (2026). The effect of web-based learning with peer-facilitated discussion on nursing students’ knowledge and practices in work-related biological exposure: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09333-1
title: Knowledge, Attitude/Belief, and Practice (KAP) model as an explanatory framework for behavior change in occupational protection
description: The article employs the KAP model to explain how knowledge and attitudes influence actual behaviors in occupational protection contexts. Knowledge forms the cornerstone of behavior development, and only when knowledge transcends into belief can individuals embrace a positive attitude toward modifying practices. The authors use this framework to interpret why the intervention improved both knowledge and behaviors simultaneously.
requirements: Learners must acquire sufficient knowledge before it can translate into beliefs and behavior change
constraints: The authors present the KAP model as an interpretive framework rather than a tested mechanism in this study
target_learning_goals: Translating occupational protection knowledge into safer clinical practices
examples: The authors speculate that web-based learning permits repetitive learning while peer teaching fosters positive beliefs or attitudes, generating a synergistic effect on educational outcomes.

article_title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of medical students at a Chinese university toward virtual simulation experimental training: a cross-sectional survey of self-perceived experience.
citation: Xia Qing, Bu Juanjuan, Zuo Hang, Wang Jie, Hou Yuesong, Wang Jinian, Wu Xiaoli. (2026). Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of medical students at a Chinese university toward virtual simulation experimental training: a cross-sectional survey of self-perceived experience. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08803-w
title: KAP framework for analyzing how knowledge and attitudes translate into learning-practice behaviors in virtual simulation
description: The Knowledge, Attitude and Practice (KAP) framework is applied to assess how medical students' cognition and perceptions of virtual simulation training relate to their actual engagement. The article contrasts it with the Technology Acceptance Model, noting KAP "provides a more comprehensive behavioral perspective by integrating cognitive understanding, attitudinal disposition, and actual behavioral engagement". The study operationalizes it as three questionnaire dimensions (K1–K5, A1–A5, P1–P5) and models attitude as a mediator between knowledge and practice.
requirements: A validated multi-dimensional questionnaire measuring knowledge, attitude, and practice separately (this study's scale had Cronbach's alpha 0.912 and KMO 0.907)
constraints: The article notes the cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences; the framework's directional claims require longitudinal testing
target_learning_goals: engagement in virtual simulation clinical skills training
technology acceptance in medical education
examples: The study tested the framework's hypothesized pathway that students with higher knowledge and more positive attitudes demonstrate stronger engagement, via regression and PROCESS mediation analysis

citation: Minja, E. G., Mrimi, E. C., Mponzi, W. P., Beckmann, J., Finda, M. F., Okumu, F. O., Long, K. Z., Lang, C., Utzinger, J., & Gerber, M. (2025). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 22(9), 1335. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph22091335
title: KaziKidz school-based physical activity program
description: KaziKidz is a teaching-material program that "integrates structured PA into the regular school timetable and is designed to enhance PA levels, school satisfaction, and psychosocial well-being." In the KaziAfya trial, children in PA arms received two 45-minute PA classes per week (activities such as moving to music and physical education) delivered by trained physical education instructors supporting classroom teachers, with sessions scheduled during existing free periods.
requirements: Trained physical education instructors to support classroom teachers and ensure fidelity of implementation
Compatibility with the existing school curriculum and adequate facilities for physical education classes
constraints: Large class sizes and a limited number of trained sports teachers may restrict the intensity and quality of lessons in Tanzanian public primary schools
target_learners: primary schoolchildren in resource-limited public schools
target_learning_goals: physical activity levels
school satisfaction
psychosocial well-being
examples: In KaziAfya, PA sessions ran twice weekly for 45 minutes from February 2020 through November 2021, resumed after a roughly 6-month COVID-19 suspension

article_title: Validating high-fidelity simulation for assessing procedural skills in nursing education: a kane framework approach in Ghana.
citation: Ntumi Simon. (2025). Validating high-fidelity simulation for assessing procedural skills in nursing education: a kane framework approach in Ghana. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07724-4
title: Kane's Validity Framework as the organizing structure for validating simulation-based assessments
description: The Kane Validity Framework is an argument-based approach that conceptualizes validation as a chain of inferences. The article states it "structures the validation process around four key inferences scoring, generalization, extrapolation, and implications each of which must be supported by empirical evidence." The study applies it to high-fidelity simulation-based assessments in Ghanaian nursing education, mapping reliability evidence to scoring, simulation–OSCE correlation to generalization, practicum prediction to extrapolation, and pass/fail consistency to implication.
requirements: Each of the four inferences must be supported with empirical evidence and logical reasoning
constraints: The article notes no published study in Ghana had previously applied this framework to high-fidelity simulation assessments for procedural skills
target_learners: final-year nursing students in diploma and bachelor's degree programs
target_learning_goals: procedural clinical competence
clinical readiness for licensure
examples: The study gathered quantitative evidence for each of the four inferences using simulation rubric scores, OSCE scores, and clinical practicum evaluations from 150 students
key_sources: Ntumi Simon. (2025). Validating high-fidelity simulation for assessing procedural skills in nursing education: a kane framework approach in Ghana. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07724-4

article_title: Students'psychological patterns and academic performance in public secondary schools in Kazo District, Uganda: a quantitative analysis.
citation: Aja Lucy, Odhine Innocent Sunday, Muhammad Tukur, Lubega Mohammad. (2025). Students' psychological patterns and academic performance in public secondary schools in Kazo District, Uganda: a quantitative analysis. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03187-w
title: Self-developed, expert-validated student questionnaire with Cronbach's alpha reliability of 0.842
description: The instrument was "a self-developed questionnaire, and it was not previously published," with the full version included as supplementary material. Five specialists in educational administration and management evaluated the items for consistency, relevance, and clarity against the study objectives. A pilot study with 50 respondents was conducted, and "The investigation, utilizing Cronbach's alpha, produced a reliability index of 0.842 for the students' questionnaire," exceeding the authors' benchmark of α = 0.70. The questionnaire contained ten Likert-scale items for each of three constructs: self-efficacy, motivation, and anxiety/stress.
requirements: Validated by five specialists in educational administration and management
Piloted with 50 respondents before full administration
constraints: Self-developed and not previously published; the full questionnaire appears only as supplementary material
target_learners: public secondary school students in Kazo District, Uganda (ages 16-18, senior 5 and 6)
target_learning_goals: measuring students' self-efficacy, motivation, and academic anxiety
examples: Administered to 254 sampled students, with 228 questionnaires returned (90.1% response rate); respondents were 135 male (59%) and 93 female (41%)

article_title: Knowledge, attitude, and practice of frailty management among clinical nurses: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Huang Xueyan, Zhou Haifang, Feng Ying, Li Mengchi, Wang Rui, Fang Ge, Lu Lumeng, Chen Jian'ao, Jiang Wenhui. (2025). Knowledge, attitude, and practice of frailty management among clinical nurses: a cross-sectional study. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-025-05776-1
title: Knowledge-Attitude-Practice (KAP) model applied to nurses' frailty management, with attitudes mediating the translation of knowledge into practice
description: The KAP model, first proposed in the 1960s, is a behavioral-change framework the article applies to nurses' frailty management. The article states that "This theoretical model classifies changes in human behavior into three stages: acquiring knowledge, generating beliefs, and forming behaviors", where knowledge is understanding and cognition, attitude is beliefs and approaches, and practice is behaviors. The article hypothesizes that "attitudes mediate translation of knowledge into practice" and tests this with structural equation modeling, finding a partial mediating effect of attitude on the knowledge-to-practice pathway.
requirements: Requires measurement of knowledge, attitude, and practice as distinct dimensions, as in the study's 31-item three-dimension questionnaire
constraints: The article notes the cross-sectional design means causal relationships among knowledge, attitudes, and practices cannot be directly inferred
target_learning_goals: Frailty screening, assessment, and management knowledge, attitudes, and practices
examples: The study used the KAP model to structure a 31-item questionnaire and a structural equation model of 524 nurses' frailty-management knowledge, attitudes, and practices.
key_sources: Huang Xueyan, Zhou Haifang, Feng Ying, Li Mengchi, Wang Rui, Fang Ge, Lu Lumeng, Chen Jian'ao, Jiang Wenhui. (2025). Knowledge, attitude, and practice of frailty management among clinical nurses: a cross-sectional study. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-025-05776-1

article_title: Bringing theory to life: integrating case-based learning in applied physiology for undergraduate physiotherapy education.
citation: Elgheit Rehab E. Abo, Nashat Nagwa. (2025). Bringing theory to life: integrating case-based learning in applied physiology for undergraduate physiotherapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06725-7
title: Kaddoura five-step CBL session structure for applied physiology labs
description: A reusable session-level design for case-based learning in which the facilitator guides students through five ordered phases. The article states: "The Kaddoura method includes five sequential steps: case presentation, presentation of triggering questions by the facilitators, creating a comfortable and safe atmosphere for learners, active participation of all students in discussions, and finally case summarization by the facilitator." Sessions began with an interactive introduction to the physiology topic, and learning objectives aligned with course outcomes were shared with students at the start of each session.
requirements: Trained facilitators who act as guides rather than teachers and formulate triggering questions that stimulate critical thinking
Cases aligned with session ILOs and course learning outcomes, with objectives shared with students at session start
target_learners: undergraduate physiotherapy students in a fourth-semester neuroscience course
target_learning_goals: applying theoretical physiology knowledge to clinical case scenarios
critical thinking and clinical discussion skills
examples: Weekly CBL sessions were run in the lab component of the applied physiology course, with students in small batches of about six students per facilitator using this five-step structure

article_title: Development and validation of situational judgement test for assessment of behavioural competencies required for effective medical practice in Nigeria.
citation: Obi Uche Shalom, Chukwuma Adanna, Agu Ifunanya, Eigbiremolen Godstime, Mbachu Chinyere. (2024). Development and validation of situational judgement test for assessment of behavioural competencies required for effective medical practice in Nigeria. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06298-x
title: Kane's validity argument framework for interpreting test scores
description: Kane's framework treats validation as a sequence: first determining the use and interpretation of assessment scores, then deriving assumptions from that use, then testing the weakest assumptions by gathering evidence for four inferences in order - scoring, generalization, extrapolation and implication. The article uses it to structure validation of the SJT, noting that unlike other frameworks it "captures evidence related to the measured construct and evidence related to job prediction performance" and specifies the order for collecting validity evidence. In this study only the scoring and generalization inferences were tested.
requirements: Validation proceeds stepwise: a clear statement of proposed score use and interpretation must precede evidence gathering, and the weakest assumptions of the validity argument are tested first.
constraints: The article notes "Kane’s framework has its limitations", and that at this stage of evidence gathering it is inappropriate to assume the findings justify the proposed score use until extrapolation and implication inferences are addressed.
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of behavioural competencies required for medical practice
examples: The authors stated that high SJT scores would reflect good behavioural competence, assumed higher scorers possess competencies linked to better healthcare provision, and gathered scoring and generalization evidence from 303 trainees.
key_sources: Obi Uche Shalom, Chukwuma Adanna, Agu Ifunanya, Eigbiremolen Godstime, Mbachu Chinyere. (2024). Development and validation of situational judgement test for assessment of behavioural competencies required for effective medical practice in Nigeria. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06298-x

article_title: Competence and Training Needs in Infectious Disease Emergency Response Among Chinese Nurses: Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Zhang Dandan, Chen Yong-Jun, Cui Tianxin, Zhang Jianzhong, Chen Si-Ying, Zhang Yin-Ping. (2024). Competence and Training Needs in Infectious Disease Emergency Response Among Chinese Nurses: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Public Health and Surveillance. https://doi.org/10.2196/62887
title: Health care workers' infectious disease emergency response competence questionnaire (Kan, 2018)
description: A self-assessment questionnaire developed by Kan in 2018 measuring infectious disease emergency response competence in three dimensions: prevention, preparedness, and response competence, with "3 primary, 11 secondary, and 36 tertiary indicators" scored on a 5-point Likert scale (total 36-180). In this study the Cronbach α was 0.93 and the content validity index 0.87. It was used to survey 2055 Chinese nurses across 80 hospitals.
requirements: Respondents are registered nurses with over 1 year of clinical experience completing a validated self-assessment instrument
constraints: Scores are self-assessments, which the authors note may be influenced by social desirability effects and recall bias
target_learners: Registered nurses in Chinese public hospitals
target_learning_goals: Infectious disease emergency response competence (prevention, preparedness, and response)
examples: Administered online via Sojump with WeChat distribution to 2213 nurses, yielding 2055 valid questionnaires after exclusions

article_title: Associations between an open-response situational judgment test and performance on OSCEs and fieldwork: implications for admissions decisions and matriculant diversity in an occupational therapy program.
citation: Roduta Roberts Mary, Alves Cecilia Brito, Chen Fu, St. Jean Craig Richard. (2024). Associations between an open-response situational judgment test and performance on OSCEs and fieldwork: implications for admissions decisions and matriculant diversity in an occupational therapy program. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06071-0
title: Kane's validation framework applied to admissions test use (interpretation-use argument with extrapolation and implication inferences)
description: The study positions itself within contemporary assessment validation, in which "validation entails two steps": articulating key claims in an interpretation-use argument, then developing a validity argument to test them. Inferences move through scoring, generalization, extrapolation, and implication stages, directing collection of Messick's validity evidence types. This study prioritized extrapolation (associations between Casper and OSCE/fieldwork performance) and implication (demographic consequences of weighting Casper) inferences, leaving scoring and generalization to the test developer's manual.
requirements: Evaluation of scoring and generalization inferences must be undertaken by the test developer prior to administration
constraints: Evidence for extrapolation and implication requires student data from programs already using the test in admissions
target_learners: admissions committees and assessment researchers in health professions education
target_learning_goals: building and evaluating validity arguments for selection instrument use
examples: The study evaluated the central claim that Casper can inform admissions decisions selecting a diverse cohort with high potential for practice-based activities requiring non-academic skills

Associations between an open-response situational judgment test and performance on OSCEs and fieldwork: implications for admissions decisions and matriculant diversity in an occupational therapy program. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06071-0

article_title: Psychological Safety Competency Training During the Clinical Internship From the Perspective of Health Care Trainee Mentors in 11 Pan-European Countries: Mixed Methods Observational Study.
citation: Irene Carrillo, Ivana Skoumalová, Ireen Bruus, Victoria Klemm, Sofia Guerra-Paiva, Bojana Knežević, Augustina Jankauskiene, Dragana Jocic, Susanna Tella, Sandra C Buttigieg, Einav Srulovici, Andrea Madarasová Gecková, Kaja Põlluste, Reinhard Strametz, Paulo Sousa, Marina Odalovic, José Joaquín Mira. (2024). Psychological Safety Competency Training During the Clinical Internship From the Perspective of Health Care Trainee Mentors in 11 Pan-European Countries: Mixed Methods Observational Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64125
title: First framework specifying observable psychological safety competencies for health care trainees (KAS items)
description: The study developed an ad hoc 29-item questionnaire operationalizing psychological safety competencies across knowledge (7 items), attitudes (6 items), and skills (7 items), plus 9 institutional intervention items, drawing on validated instruments for psychological safety, speaking up, and patient safety competencies. The authors state their framework is "the first to specify what a competent trainee in psychological safety would look like, exemplifying not only what they should know and feel (aspects that are not directly observable) but also what they should do and what others can observe to evaluate their competence." Items cover assertive warning, constructive response to negative reactions, peer support for second victims, and expressing improvement proposals.
requirements: Items were translated and back-translated for participating countries; readability and face validity were tested with 3 mentors per country before use
constraints: The instrument is ad hoc; the authors note no prior instruments explicitly define psychological safety competencies
target_learners: health care trainees assessed via their mentors' ratings
target_learning_goals: psychological safety competencies across knowledge, attitudes, and skills domains
examples: Sample skill item: offer peer support to a colleague involved in an adverse event to reduce the second victim syndrome, characterized by feelings of guilt, inadequacy, anxiety, shame, hypervigilance, or grief

article_title: Evaluating clinical communication skills of medical students, assistants, and professors.
citation: Moezzi Masoumeh, Rasekh Sara, Zare Elahe, Karimi Masoud. (2024). Evaluating clinical communication skills of medical students, assistants, and professors. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-05015-4
title: KAP questionnaire battery for clinical communication skills (knowledge, CSAS attitude, and performance questionnaires)
description: A three-instrument battery used to assess knowledge, attitude, and performance regarding clinical communication skills among medical students, assistants, and professors. It comprises a researcher-made 10-item knowledge questionnaire (score range 0-10), the 26-item Communication Skills Attitude Questionnaire (CSAS) with positive and negative subscales, and a 28-item communication skills performance questionnaire scored 28-140. Validity was checked by expert panels (CVR > 0.78, CVI > 0.79) and reliability by Cronbach's alpha (0.90, 0.70, 0.75) and test-retest on a pilot sample of 30 subjects.
requirements: Administered with informed consent; content validity confirmed by panels of health promotion and medical education experts
constraints: Self-administered; the authors note responses may be biased by social desirability because skills were not directly observed
target_learning_goals: assessment of clinical communication skills knowledge, attitude, and performance
examples: Used in the 2019 cross-sectional study at Shahrekord University of Medical Sciences hospitals with 289 respondents

article_title: Effects of a school-based karate intervention on academic achievement, psychosocial functioning, and physical fitness: A multi-country cluster randomized controlled trial.
citation: Pinto-Escalona Tania, Gobbi Erica, Valenzuela Pedro L., Bennett Simon J., Aschieri Pierluigi, Martin-Loeches Manuel, Paoli Antonio, Martinez-de-Quel Oscar. (2024). Effects of a school-based karate intervention on academic achievement, psychosocial functioning, and physical fitness: A multi-country cluster randomized controlled trial. Journal of Sport and Health Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jshs.2021.10.006
title: Karate Mind and Movement program
description: The Karate Mind and Movement program is a school-based karate intervention delivered by certified karate technicians during PE lessons, 2 h/week for one academic year, replacing habitual PE activities. Sessions created "an enriched environment was created in school gyms using tatamis" with modular materials, and included barefoot movements for body awareness, balance and coordination, non-specific motor tasks, stretching, and class discussion. It was evaluated in the Sport at School cluster randomized trial.
requirements: Delivered by black-belt, karate-teaching-certified technicians who completed a 2-week (40 h/week) training course with continuous online support from project coordinators
Implemented within PE lesson time so an equal amount of time is spent as in habitual PE lessons
constraints: The article notes intensity was not monitored, so improvements could not be attributed to higher exercise intensity versus exercise specificity/variability
target_learners: Primary school children aged 7–8 years (second grade)
target_learning_goals: Basic motor skills development
Cardiorespiratory fitness, balance and flexibility
Cognitive performance and collaboration during physical education
examples: In the Sport at School trial, 388 children in the intervention group received the program across 20 schools in 5 European countries during the 2017–2018 academic year.
